# generator-shortcuts

**Question:** For this generator, name the strongest plausible shortcut or rival rule that fits the canonical demonstrations. Give an exact input on which it disagrees with the intended rule, how you checked the output, and whether your proposed generator emits such cases.

## Strongest surviving domain shortcut: all-or-nothing clipping

A plausible rival performs the same local grouping, seed interpretation and reflection, but **skips an entire reflected copy if any cell would leave the grid**. The canonical authority clips cells individually instead. This rival fits all eight canonical pair records (four unique inputs), and it agrees on the whole deliberately unclipped generator domain. It is therefore stronger than ordinary translation or global seed-frequency rivals, which generated examples can refute.

The exact witness is a **12-row × 12-column** input, initially all zero, with precisely these six nonzero cells (zero-based row, column, color):

| Row | Column | Color |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 | 2 |
| 1 | 0 | 3 |
| 1 | 1 | 4 |
| 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 2 | 1 | 4 |
| 3 | 1 | 4 |

Canonical output has the same 12×12 shape. It retains those cells and adds exactly `(0,2)=2`, `(2,0)=3`, and `(3,0)=3`. The rival output is the unchanged input, because both reflected blocks partially leave the canvas. The complete grids and predictions are retained in `checks/canonical-diagnostics/inputs.json`, `case_manifest.json`, and `rival_outputs.json`.

## How the labels were checked

The retained prior audit `review-5e3868cd57b705df:v0001` was a lead, not proof of the current result. I rebuilt its literal input and its translation by (+3,+3), then ran fresh public `arcpuzzles apply dc2c4869445c` on both and all eight canonical records. The Racket receipt is `checks/canonical-diagnostics/racket.json`; `comparison.json` shows the three exact disagreements, agreement on the interior control and all canonical records, and agreement with the independent Python mirror on all ten records. `probe.py` reproduces the observations and source identity checks.

The canonical raw `program_solution` SHA-256 is `bf88e8ff998e82775552a9164adcc733433cf5fc60a9df43afa1467a4106b49f`. The public executable wrapper is a different byte sequence with SHA-256 `4f9e1757d2fb7d1360948dfa342feebdee6f8626f40cef3d88dfaeb989ddfe26`. The whitespace-normalized raw rule pin remains `f9fbf72b057d`. These identities are distinguished explicitly rather than treating different wrappers as the same text.

## Does this return generate the witness?

**No.** The selected generator and its compact placement fallback continue to require whole reflection blocks in bounds and collision-free. `self_check` rejects this edge witness with `reflection block clips the grid edge`; the (+3,+3) translated control is accepted. The gap prototype is even more conservative: it requires valid placement at all three gap settings. The lesson curator works within the same accepted domain. Neither can teach the distinction between partial clipping and skipping an entire clipped copy.

This is an explicit domain limitation, not an in-domain label defect. I did not silently broaden the generator or change the canonical authority to erase the discrepancy. A future clipping extension would need its own deliberate input support, overlap/paint-order decision, and lessons that demonstrate partial copies. The pre-existing audit remains a domain question for the maintainer; this return does not mark it resolved.

Separately, the larger canonical lesson census found real in-domain ambiguity against the global-singleton-seed rival. Exact failed lessons are retained and the new lesson curator supplies replacement demonstrations checked against both declared rivals. That finite improvement does not address the excluded clipping branch or establish uniqueness against all possible hypotheses.
